case_info.scenario: A right-handed man in his 50s with a history of hepatitis C presented to clinic with a 1-year history of an enlarging painless nodule on his right index finger, which was now causing destruction of his nail. No preceding trauma was reported. On examination, an erythematous 15 × 10-mm well-circumscribed lobulated firm nodule was seen extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate of the right index finger, causing destruction of the adjacent nail plate (Figure 1A). The lesion did not transilluminate. No other findings were noted on full skin examination. A radiograph of the right hand revealed erosion of the distal phalanx, and 4-mm punch biopsies were taken from the proximal and distal pole of the nodule, highlighting similar histological features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, well-circumscribed, lobulated firm nodule extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate on the right index finger. Local invasion from the tumor has caused resultant lifting of the overlying nail plate, which appears thinned, split and shortened, failing to cover the distal nail bed. B, Punch biopsy showing acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion.
case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, well-circumscribed, lobulated firm nodule extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate on the right index finger. Local invasion from the tumor has caused resultant lifting of the overlying nail plate, which appears thinned, split and shortened, failing to cover the distal nail bed. case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.scenario: A right-handed man in his 50s with a history of hepatitis C presented to clinic with a 1-year history of an enlarging painless nodule on his right index finger, which was now causing destruction of his nail. No preceding trauma was reported. On examination, an erythematous 15 × 10-mm well-circumscribed lobulated firm nodule was seen extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate of the right index finger, causing destruction of the adjacent nail plate (Figure 1A). The lesion did not transilluminate. No other findings were noted on full skin examination. A radiograph of the right hand revealed erosion of the distal phalanx, and 4-mm punch biopsies were taken from the proximal and distal pole of the nodule, highlighting similar histological features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, well-circumscribed, lobulated firm nodule extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate on the right index finger. Local invasion from the tumor has caused resultant lifting of the overlying nail plate, which appears thinned, split and shortened, failing to cover the distal nail bed. B, Punch biopsy showing acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion.
case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

Local invasion from the tumor has caused resultant lifting of the overlying nail plate, which appears thinned, split and shortened, failing to cover the distal nail bed. case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

You MUST pick a stage from this list.

On examination, an erythematous 15 × 10-mm well-circumscribed lobulated firm nodule was seen extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate of the right index finger, causing destruction of the adjacent nail plate (Figure 1A). case_info.caption: A, Erythematous, well-circumscribed, lobulated firm nodule extending from the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint to the nail plate on the right index finger. Local invasion from the tumor has caused resultant lifting of the overlying nail plate, which appears thinned, split and shortened, failing to cover the distal nail bed. case_info.explanation: C. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor Histopathological analysis revealed acral skin with a well-circumscribed lobular dermal lesion (Figure 1B). On higher power, xanthoma cells and hemosiderin deposition are seen, with bland mononuclear cells forming osteoclastlike giant cells focally (Figure 2). The patient was referred to plastic surgery for complete resection. Tenosynovial giant cell tumors (TGCTs; previously known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath) are a rare, locally aggressive, mesenchymal tumor arising from the joints, bursa, and tendon sheaths. They can present with attacks of pain, swelling, arthritis and spontaneous hemarthrosis. TGCTs are more common in female individuals, with a mean age at diagnosis of 35 to 50 years.1They tend to occur on volar aspects of fingers, near the distal interphalangeal joint.2Generally these are benign tumors, with sarcomatous transformation and metastatic spread being exceedingly rare.1However, they have a destructive potential, as exemplified inFigure 1A, showing the tumor abutting and infiltrating the proximal nail fold causing adjacent nail plate distortion and destruction. These destructive tendencies can negatively impact a person’s functioning and quality of life. Up to 50% of TGCTs can result in nail plate changes, with onycholysis being a frequent finding.3 Clinically, they can be subdivided into nodular (N-TGCT), as in the present case, or diffuse TGCT (D-TGCT). N-TGCT usually presents as a single lesion arising near tendons or interphalangeal joints, often evolving over years, with the potential to erode bone or overlying skin. D-TGCT shows more extensive, infiltrative involvement and can extend into extra-articular structures with severe disability. Recurrences are lower in N-TGCT at about 10%, compared to 70% in D-TGCT.1Higher recurrence rates are observed in tumors with multiple satellite nodules and closer proximity to the interphalangeal joints. Meticulous dissection ensuring complete excision has been shown to reduce the risk of recurrence.4 It is important to consider amelanotic melanoma in the differential diagnosis of a rapidly enlarging skin-colored or slightly erythematous nodule. Approximate 2% to 8% of all melanomas are amelanotic, with no pigment on visual or histological examination.5Histopathology is varied, but nodular subtypes are most frequent.6Compared to pigmented melanomas, amelanotic melanomas are associated with older age at diagnosis and are predominantly found in White skin types.5Additionally, they have a higher risk of delayed diagnosis and a significant lower 5-year melanoma-specific survival compared to pigmented melanoma. They tend to affect intermittent sun-exposed body areas more frequently. Common dermoscopic features include white structureless zones, linear looped vessels, linear irregular vessels, and arborizing vessels.7 A cellular digital fibroma is another differential for an asymptomatic acral tumor. This is a benign fibrous tumor that would classically present as an erythematous or a skin-colored papule, often smaller (usually less than 5 mm) than the lesion described in the present case. Typically, it is located on the lateral, dorsal, or ventral aspect of the digit and less commonly affecting the proximal nail fold. Histology would highlight prominent cellular proliferation of spindle-shaped fibroblasts in the dermis and without erosion of the tumor into the bony phalanx. Immunohistochemistry testing would reveal strongly positive CD34 staining throughout the lesion.8 Similar to TGCT, a plexiform fibrohistiocytic tumor (PFHT) is another mesenchymal tumor of intermediate malignancy. It does have a predilection for the distal upper extremities but would generally present in children and young adults as a solitary, indolent, slow-growing dermal or subcutaneous nodule. Overlying skin is slightly raised, and a central depression may be present. The etiopathogenesis of PFHT is unknown, but it is thought that preceding trauma may play a role.9Similar to a TGCT, histology would highlight osteoclastlike multinucleated giant cells. However classically, PFHT is a biphasic tumor and would also consist of nodules of histiocytelike cells surrounded by cellular fascicles of myofibroblasts.10
